narration: For decades, the deal in America was simple. One job could buy a house, a car, raise a couple of kids, and still put something away for retirement.
caption: the old deal

narration: They called it the American Dream — the promise that anyone who worked hard could attain a better life.
For a huge share of the country, that promise is quietly breaking. And the data shows it happening in slow motion.
In 1971, around sixty-one percent of American adults lived in middle-income households. Today it's closer to fifty. The middle is emptying out.
sub: share of US adults in the middle class (Pew)

narration: And here's the part nobody shows you. It's not just shrinking. It's splitting — a few rising to the top, more sliding down.
caption: the middle is hollowing out

narration: So let's follow the numbers. Why is the middle class disappearing — and what's actually taking its place?
heading: Why the Middle Class Is Disappearing
sub: It didn't vanish. It got squeezed.

narration: First — what even is the middle class? Weirdly, almost nobody agrees.
Technically it's just the people in the middle of the income ladder — not rich, not poor.
But the definitions are so loose that by some measures it's a quarter of households, and by others, three-quarters.
So let's use a clean one, from the Pew Research Center. Middle class means a household earning between two-thirds and double the national median income.
But 'middle class' was never really about a precise number. It was about a feeling — security. A home, healthcare, retirement, and kids who'd do better than you.
And you can watch that security erode, decade by decade. One income to two. A starter home to a bidding war. A degree that was free-ish to one that costs a fortune.
title: The same life, getting harder to afford

narration: That feeling — not the salary — is what's really disappearing. And three big forces are pulling it apart.
The first force is the one you can feel every single month: the squeeze.
heading: Force One: The Squeeze

narration: Start with your paycheck. What matters isn't the number on it — it's what that number can actually buy. Real wages.
For decades after the war, as workers produced more each hour, their pay climbed right alongside it. Produce more, earn more.
Then, around the 1970s, that line split in two. The economy kept getting more productive — but the typical worker's pay flattened out.
title: Productivity kept climbing. Pay didn't.

narration: That growing gap between what workers produced and what they were paid became, quite simply, someone else's profit.
Now squeeze that flat paycheck from the other side. Because the things a middle-class life actually requires did not stay flat. They exploded.
caption: flat wages, rising costs

narration: Look at what's happened to prices since the 1980s. Televisions and gadgets got cheaper. But the pillars of a stable life ran away from wages completely.
title: Price growth since the 1980s (%)

narration: Housing — the single biggest cost — has raced ahead of incomes for decades.
Healthcare in America costs far more than almost anywhere else on Earth.
And the college degree that once guaranteed a middle-class life now often comes attached to decades of debt.
Housing, healthcare, childcare, college — the exact pillars of a middle-class life are the ones whose prices ran away fastest.
caption: one paycheck, four exploding costs

narration: Which led straight to force two. When one income stopped stretching, families did the obvious thing — they sent two people to work.
heading: Force Two: Running to Stand Still

narration: But a bankruptcy expert named Elizabeth Warren spotted the trap hiding inside that fix.
label: Elizabeth Warren
caption: …who named the trap

narration: Her research found that two-income families were ending up more financially fragile, not less.
Why? Because once most families had two earners, the price of what they competed for — especially houses in good school districts — simply rose to soak up that second income.
caption: two incomes — still treading water

narration: So now it takes two incomes to afford what one used to. And with both parents working, a single job loss or one illness can sink the entire ship.
So how did families cover the gap in the meantime? Simple. They borrowed.
Credit cards, auto loans, student loans, home-equity lines. For years, debt quietly papered over the fact that the paycheck no longer reached the end of the month.
caption: debt filled the gap

narration: Which is how you get families earning six figures who still live paycheck to paycheck. The income looks middle class. The security is gone.
It can feel fine — right up until it isn't. One surprise bill, and the whole illusion wobbles.
And while the middle was being squeezed, the very top was pulling away — fast.
heading: Force Three: The Great Divergence

narration: Income inequality in America has climbed back to levels not seen since the 1920s.
And it's even sharper in wealth — what you own, not just what you earn.
The share of the country's income flowing to the middle class has been shrinking for fifty years — while the slice going to the top has swelled.
caption: the middle's slice shrinks

narration: Here's the quiet engine of it. The richest don't mostly earn a wage. They own assets — stocks, companies, real estate.
caption: the gap is ownership

narration: So when those assets boom, owners rocket away from everyone living on a salary. Over forty years, assets have massively outrun wages.
caption: assets raced ahead of pay

narration: Which means two families earning the identical salary can end up worlds apart — purely based on whether they owned a home and some stocks, or didn't.
Add it all up, and the wealth of the country is lopsided. The bottom half owns almost nothing. The top tenth owns roughly two-thirds of everything.
title: Share of US household wealth

narration: And the ladder up is getting harder to climb. Economic mobility — the odds a kid out-earns their parents — has been falling for generations.
For kids born in 1940, the chance of earning more than their parents was around ninety percent. For kids born in the 1980s, it had fallen to barely a coin flip.
caption: the next rung is missing

narration: So why did this happen? A big part of it was that a certain kind of job simply disappeared.
heading: Why It Happened

narration: The well-paid factory work that built the postwar middle class was hollowed out by deindustrialization.
Globalization and automation moved millions of those solid middle-wage jobs overseas, or handed them to machines.
caption: the middle rungs vanished

narration: What replaced them split in two: high-paid jobs for the credentialed few, and low-paid service work for everyone else. Economists call it job polarization.
caption: jobs split to the extremes

narration: The economy stopped producing middle-wage work — which was exactly the kind of job the middle class had been built on.
None of this was one villain, or one law. It was a slow drift of many forces, all quietly pushing the same way.
Flat real wages. Soaring core costs. Vanishing middle jobs. Wealth pooling at the top. Four forces, one direction — a hollowed-out middle.
Now, to be honest about it — this is not a simple tragedy.
heading: Is It All Bad?

narration: Because part of that shrinking middle didn't fall at all. It actually climbed into higher incomes.
A real chunk of the 'disappearing' middle class moved up and out the top. The upper-income group grew faster than the lower one did.
caption: some of the middle moved up

narration: And in raw cost-of-living terms, some things got dramatically better and cheaper.
A phone in your pocket today is more powerful than a 1970s mainframe — for about the price of a nice dinner. Gadgets got radically cheaper.
Here's the cruel split, though. The things that got cheaper are the gadgets. The things that got far pricier are the actual pillars of a stable life.
You can stream every film ever made — but you can't afford the house, the doctor, or the degree. We got richer in stuff, and poorer in security.
Which points at what is really disappearing here — and it isn't a dollar figure.
heading: What's Really Disappearing

narration: The middle class didn't exactly vanish. What's vanishing is the thing it really stood for — security. The simple confidence that if you worked hard, the basics were covered.
caption: security, not status

narration: Because the American Dream was never really about getting rich. It was the quiet promise that your kids would do better than you.
And that promise, measured in cold data, has faded from near-certain to little better than a coin flip.
sub: odds a kid out-earns their parents today

narration: So when the rung you're standing on cracks, climbing to the next one stops feeling like effort — and starts feeling like luck.
caption: the promise is cracking

narration: But here's the genuinely hopeful part. None of this was a law of nature. It was built by choices — about wages, housing, healthcare, education, and taxes.
A middle class isn't something a country just has. It's a promise a society chooses to keep — or quietly lets slide.
caption: it rests on a promise

narration: So the next time someone says the middle class is 'disappearing,' you'll know it isn't vanishing into thin air. It's being squeezed, split, and priced out.
